Few people could claim a heart so pure, or such genuine humility combined with a firm confidence in their own integrity and faith in the integrity of others. She had lived a secluded life from birth. Her mother died when she was very young, but her father devoted himself to her education. He held many unusual ideas, which shaped the system he chose for teaching her. She knew a great deal about the heroes of Greece and Rome, and those of England who had lived centuries earlier, yet knew almost nothing about current events. She had read few authors from at least the past fifty years, although apart from that exception her reading was extensive. Thus, while she appeared less familiar than he was with the mysteries of life and society, her knowledge ran deeper and rested on stronger foundations. Even if her beauty and gentleness had not captivated him, her intelligence would always have held his own in its power. He looked up to her as his guide, and adored her so much that he delighted in deepening, in his own mind, the feeling of inferiority she sometimes inspired.

His mother died when he was nineteen. He left college after her death and, distancing himself for a time from his old friends, withdrew to the neighbourhood where his Diana lived. All his comfort came from her gentle voice and her still more precious caresses. This brief separation from his companions gave him the courage to assert his independence. He felt that, however much they might ridicule his proposed marriage, they would not dare display their ridicule once it had taken place. He therefore sought his guardian’s consent, which he obtained with some difficulty, and that of his beloved’s father, which was granted more readily. Without telling anyone else of his plans, he became Diana’s husband by the time he reached his twentieth birthday.

He loved her passionately, and her tenderness had such a hold on him that he could think of nothing else. He invited some college friends to visit, but their frivolity disgusted him. Diana had torn away the veil that had kept him a boy: he had become a man. He wondered how he could ever have shared his fellow students’ empty phrases and ideas, or for a single moment have feared the criticism of such people. He abandoned his old friendships not because he was inconstant, but because they were truly unworthy of him.

Emma Woodhouse, good-looking, intelligent, and wealthy, possessing a pleasant home and a cheerful temper, appeared to combine several of life’s greatest blessings. She had spent almost twenty-one years in the world with scarcely anything to trouble or distress her.

She was the younger of two daughters of a very loving and indulgent father, and her sister’s marriage had made her mistress of his household at an early age. Her mother had died so long before that only a vague recollection of her caresses remained. An excellent woman, employed as governess, had taken her place and had scarcely fallen short of a mother in her affection.

Miss Taylor had belonged to Mr. Woodhouse’s household for sixteen years, more a friend than a governess, loving both girls dearly, but Emma especially. Their closeness resembled that of sisters. Even while Miss Taylor still nominally held the post of governess, her gentle disposition had scarcely permitted her to exercise restraint. Now that even the appearance of authority had long disappeared, they lived together as deeply attached friends, with Emma following her own inclinations. She valued Miss Taylor’s judgment highly, but was governed principally by her own.

The actual drawbacks of Emma’s circumstances were, indeed, her ability to get her own way rather too often and her tendency to hold a somewhat excessive opinion of herself. These were the disadvantages that threatened to diminish her many pleasures. At present, however, she was so entirely unaware of the danger that she did not regard them as misfortunes at all.

Sorrow arrived—a mild sorrow—but it took no form of unpleasant self-awareness. Miss Taylor married. Losing Miss Taylor first introduced her to grief. On her dear friend’s wedding day, Emma sat for the first time in prolonged melancholy reflection. Once the ceremony was finished and the bridal company had departed, she and her father were left to dine alone, with no expectation of a third person to enliven the long evening. After dinner her father settled himself to sleep, as he usually did, leaving her with nothing to do but consider her loss.

The marriage promised every happiness to her friend. Mr. Weston possessed an irreproachable character, a comfortable fortune, a suitable age, and agreeable manners. Emma found some satisfaction in remembering the generous, self-denying friendship with which she had always desired and encouraged the match. Yet for her it had been a dismal morning’s work. Miss Taylor’s absence would be felt each hour of every day. She remembered all her former kindness—the affection and kindness of sixteen years—how she had taught her and played with her since she was five, how she had used every power to win her affection and entertain her when she was well, and how she had nursed her through the various illnesses of childhood.

“Will you play?”

“I believe, sir,” said the spy, turning with the most abject manner toward Mr. Lorry, “that I may ask a gentleman of your age and kindness to suggest to this other gentleman, who is so much younger, whether playing that Ace he mentioned could ever be consistent with his position. I acknowledge that I am a spy, and that the occupation is held in disrepute—though someone must undertake it. But this gentleman is no spy; why should he lower himself by becoming one?”

“Within a very few minutes, Mr. Barsad,” said Carton, answering for himself and consulting his watch, “I shall play my Ace without the slightest hesitation.”

“I would have hoped, gentlemen,” said the spy, still trying to draw Mr. Lorry into the exchange, “that your regard for my sister—”

“I could offer no better proof of my regard for your sister than to rid her, finally, of her brother,” Sydney Carton replied.

“You truly think so, sir?”

“My mind is quite settled on that point.”

The spy’s polished manner, oddly at variance with his ostentatiously coarse clothing and probably with his ordinary behaviour, was so checked by Carton’s impenetrability—he had puzzled men wiser and more honest than this one—that it wavered and deserted him. While he hesitated, Carton resumed his earlier appearance of studying cards and said:

“Indeed, upon further reflection, I strongly suspect that I hold another good card which I have not yet counted. That friend and fellow-Sheep of yours, who described himself as grazing in the country prisons—who was he?”

“A Frenchman. You do not know him,” the spy answered quickly.

“French, is he?” Carton repeated thoughtfully, apparently paying him no attention despite echoing his words. “Well, perhaps he is.”

“He is, I assure you,” said the spy, “though it is of no importance.”

“Though it is of no importance,” Carton repeated with the same mechanical air. “Though it is of no importance—no, it is not important. No. But I recognise the face.”

“I do not think so. I am certain you do not. It is impossible,” said the spy.

“It—is—impossible,” murmured Sydney Carton, searching his memory and again toying with his glass, which was fortunately small. “Impossible. He spoke French well. Yet I thought he sounded foreign?”

“A provincial accent,” said the spy.

“No, foreign!” exclaimed Carton, bringing his open palm down on the table as understanding flashed upon him. “Cly! In disguise, but the very same man. That man appeared before us at the Old Bailey.”

“Now you are being hasty, sir,” Barsad replied with a smile that tilted his hooked nose still further to one side. “There you really place an advantage in my hands.”
